after: ## Finding issues at global, national and local level
alt: A timeline of commitments: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights Article 26 (1948), the World Conference on Education for All in Jomtien (1990), Pakistan’s Article 25-A (2010) and Sustainable Development Goal 4 (2015). These are strong evidence of promises but weak evidence of what happens in classrooms; enrolment and completion data are needed.
caption: A law or goal shows what was promised, not what happens.

alt: A balance weighs low-fee private schools. Supporters: they open quickly where the state lacks schools, give choice, and some parents judge the teaching better. Critics: fees exclude the poorest, quality varies, and education is a right the state should provide. A parent weighs cost against the local state school; a teacher focuses on pay, class size and training.
caption: Beyond for and against, parents and teachers judge the issue from their own position.

alt: Six possible causes surround a child out of school: cost, distance and safety, supply of schools and teachers, conflict or disaster, social expectations and disability. Below, a chain: a distant secondary school means transport costs, so poorer families keep children home and they leave with fewer qualifications.
caption: Each cause is a line of analysis to test with evidence.

alt: Four rings show consequences of missing education: personally, fewer choices of work and study; locally, fewer trained teachers and nurses; nationally, effects on the economy and informed citizens; globally, slower progress on SDG 4.
caption: Missing school affects one person, a community, a country and shared global goals.

alt: Two bars rise from 68% to 83%. The absolute change is 15 percentage points; the relative change is about a 22% rise, because 15 divided by 68 is about 0.22. Mixing the two can be careless or exaggerated.
caption: A rise from 68% to 83% is 15 percentage points but about 22% in relative terms.

alt: A fictional campaign group asked 300 parents in Marrowby why a child left school; 45% (135 parents) named fees and 55% gave other reasons. The evaluation moves from the claim, to what the evidence supports locally, to its weaknesses (one town, generalisation, under half, vested interest), to a judgement that it cannot support a national claim.
caption: Claim, evidence, what it supports, weaknesses, judgement: in that order.

after: ## Courses of action and their effects
alt: Removing school fees tackles the cost barrier and is likely to raise enrolment among the poorest families. Two limits follow: without more teachers and classrooms, class sizes rise and quality may fall; and uniforms, transport and lost income remain. Judgement: it works best in a package with teacher funding, judged by learning as well as enrolment.
caption: An action is judged by its effect, its limits, and what it needs alongside it.
